sections.title: I. Context for the team and the AI

questions.text: What should this migration move?
questions.help: Structure is the Warehouse with its schemas, empty tables, functions, views, procedures and roles. Data is each table's rows, loaded inside Fabric by data pipelines. Orchestration is the notebooks, pipelines, connections, Spark, jobs, scripts, schedules and shortcuts. Leave out what moves later.

options.label: Structure
options.description: The Warehouse, its schemas, empty tables, functions, views, procedures and roles

options.label: Data
options.description: Each table's rows, loaded by Fabric data pipelines

options.label: Orchestration
options.description: Notebooks, pipelines, connections, Spark, jobs, scripts, schedules and shortcuts

defaults.reason: {fact:objects.total} objects were discovered, and everything can move in this migration.

questions.text: Data lake storage the code reads directly: reach it through OneLake shortcuts, or leave the paths as they are?
questions.help: In Synapse the code read storage as the workspace's managed identity; in Fabric it runs as the signed-in user. A OneLake shortcut leaves the data where it is and keeps the access working: the code's paths are rewritten to go through it. Nothing is copied either way.

options.label: Through OneLake shortcuts
options.description: Every location found gets a shortcut; the data stays where it is

options.label: Leave the paths as they are
options.description: The code reads storage directly, as the signed-in user

defaults.reason: {fact:storage.locations} storage locations are read by the code directly.

questions.text: Which objects are in scope?
questions.help: Everything is the usual answer. Narrow it to some schemas and folders, or leave out objects by their names (backups, temporary copies). Plan's Add all follows this; an object can still be added by hand, and Plan says it differs from the brief.

options.label: Everything
options.description: Every object discovered

options.label: These schemas and folders only
options.description: Only the objects in the schemas and folders you choose

options.label: Everything except some names
options.description: Leave out objects whose names match patterns

defaults.reason: Nothing discovered is marked as out of scope.

questions.text: Which schemas and folders are in scope?
questions.help: SQL objects are in scope by their schema; pipelines, notebooks, scripts and the rest by the Synapse folder they are in (and folders under it).

questions.text: Which names are left out?
questions.help: Patterns matched against each object's name, ignoring case: * for any text, ? for one character.

defaults.reason: Backup and temporary copies are the usual candidates.

questions.text: Views, stored procedures and functions: bring them across, or leave them out for now?
questions.help: They are created in the Warehouse from their own definitions, after the rules have fixed what Fabric rejects. Leaving them out moves the tables (and their data) first; the rest can follow in a later run.

options.label: Bring them across
options.description: Created in the Warehouse; what the rules cannot fix is reported, or drafted with AI (D5)

options.label: Leave them out for now
options.description: Plan's Add all leaves them out of the plan

defaults.reason: {fact:code.sqlModules} views, procedures and functions were discovered.

questions.text: Scripts and pipelines written for the serverless SQL pool: leave them out, or keep them for a person?
questions.help: Fabric has no serverless SQL pool. The Lakehouse's SQL endpoint takes its place, over the shortcuts the External tables stage makes.

options.label: Leave them out
options.description: Plan's Add all leaves them out of the plan

options.label: Keep them for a person
options.description: They stay in the plan, reported for a person to rework

defaults.reason: {fact:code.serverlessObjects} objects use the serverless pool, which the Lakehouse's SQL endpoint replaces in Fabric.

questions.text: Pipelines with activities Fabric lacks (such as a mapping data flow or an SSIS package) and .NET for Spark notebooks: rebuild them by hand, or leave them out?
questions.help: They cannot be converted as they are: Fabric pipelines have no equivalent for those activities, and Fabric Spark runs no .NET. Rebuilding by hand keeps them in the plan, each with a task in the execution plan.

options.label: Rebuild them by hand
options.description: They stay in the plan, with a task for a person

options.label: Leave them out
options.description: Plan's Add all leaves them out

defaults.reason: {fact:code.unsupportedPipelines} pipelines and {fact:code.dotnetNotebooks} notebooks have no Fabric equivalent as they are.

questions.text: Who rebuilds them, and how?
How much of each table's history should load?
questions.help: A date filter loads only the newer rows of each table with a date column, on its first date column. Validate counts Synapse with the same filter.

options.label: Every row
options.description: Synapse and Fabric hold the same rows

options.label: Rows since a date
options.description: Older rows stay in Synapse

defaults.reason: {fact:tables.withDateColumn} tables have a date column. Loading every row keeps both sides identical, which Validate's row counts then show.

questions.text: Load rows since which date?
questions.help: The date is fixed in the brief, never 'two years ago', so every run loads the same rows.

questions.text: Deliver it in one run, or wave by wave?
questions.help: A run creates objects wave by wave, in dependency order. It can go straight through, stop at the end of a wave that has failures, or wait for a person to sign each wave off before the next one starts.

options.label: Straight through
options.description: Every object is attempted; failures are reported

options.label: Stop at a wave with failures
options.description: A failed table never lets the views that read it start

options.label: A person signs off each wave
options.description: The run pauses after each wave; Resume signs it off and starts the next

defaults.reason: {fact:waves.count} waves. Stopping after a wave with failures keeps a failed table from letting the views that read it start.

questions.text: Objects already in Fabric: leave them, or update them in place?
questions.help: Updating redeploys fixes and accepted LLM drafts: views and procedures by CREATE OR ALTER, notebooks, pipelines, scripts and Spark jobs by a new definition. Tables are never replaced.

options.label: Leave them
options.description: Anything already in Fabric stays as it is

options.label: Update them in place
options.description: Overwrites changes someone made in Fabric

defaults.reason: Leaving what is there makes every run safe to repeat.

separateApprover.reason: It lets runs overwrite objects that are already in Fabric.

questions.text: Which collation should the Warehouse have?
questions.help: A Warehouse's collation is set when it is created and cannot change afterwards. Each draft is told whether names and text compare with case.

options.label: Same as the Synapse pool
options.description: Case-sensitive only if the pool was

options.label: Case-insensitive
options.description: 'ABC' equals 'abc', as in most Synapse pools

options.label: Case-sensitive
options.description: Fabric's own default

defaults.reason: The Synapse pool's collation is {fact:pool.collation}.

questions.text: What should the Warehouse be called?
questions.help: Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter. A different name later creates another Warehouse.

defaults.reason: Named after the pool, {fact:pool.name}.

questions.text: What should the Lakehouse be called?
questions.help: The Lakehouse holds the OneLake shortcuts, storage routed through them, and the Spark jobs' default lakehouse.

defaults.reason: Named after the Warehouse.

questions.text: Coding standards for converted code
questions.help: Rules every AI draft follows: formatting, comments, patterns to avoid. They go to the AI with each draft, in MIGRATION_CONTEXT.md, beside the project requirements. The rule-based conversion keeps the code as close to the original as Fabric allows.

defaults.reason: None beyond the project requirements already set.

questions.text: Naming convention for anything new a draft has to create
questions.help: Existing objects keep their Synapse names. When a draft must add something (an inline function that replaces a multi-statement one, a staging table, a notebook cell), it is named this way. Sent to the AI with each draft.

questions.text: Keep tables in sync after the first load?
questions.help: A sync pipeline then loads new and changed rows on a schedule, created switched off, using each table's change column (C2) and key. A one-off migration needs none: the first load is the copy.

defaults.reason: {fact:tables.withChangeColumn} tables have a column like ModifiedAt that could drive a sync. A one-off migration needs none.

questions.text: Which column marks a changed row?
questions.help: A sync reads the rows whose change column moved since the last sync. Detected: on each table, the first date or time column named like ModifiedAt, UpdatedAt or LastModified. Named: the column you name, on every table that has it; a table without it is loaded once and not synced.

options.label: Detected on each table
options.description: A column named like ModifiedAt, UpdatedAt or LastModified

options.label: A column I name
options.description: Such as ModifiedDate, on every table that has it

defaults.reason: {fact:tables.withChangeColumn} tables have such a column.

questions.text: Which column, or columns? On each table, the first one it has is used.
questions.help: Column names, matched ignoring case, such as ModifiedDate, LastUpdated.

questions.text: Tables with a change column but no key: load them once, or append their changed rows?
questions.help: Without a key, a sync cannot tell a changed row from a new one: it can only append, so a row changed in Synapse appears twice in Fabric.

options.label: Load them once
options.description: They load with the first load and are not kept in sync

options.label: Append their changed rows
options.description: Duplicates are handled downstream

defaults.reason: {fact:tables.changeWithoutKeys} tables have a change column but no key: appending would double every changed row.

questions.text: Rows deleted in Synapse after the first load: what should happen to them in Fabric?
questions.help: A sync adds and updates rows; it cannot see a row that was deleted. They can stay in Fabric, or the synced tables can be reloaded in full at cutover, which removes them.

options.label: They stay in Fabric
options.description: Fine when rows are never deleted, or deletes do not matter downstream

options.label: Reload the synced tables at cutover
options.description: A task in the execution plan: each synced table is emptied and loaded again

defaults.reason: A sync never removes rows; most tables that change are only added to and updated.

questions.text: How far back should each sync re-read?

options.label: One hour
options.description: Catches rows committed late; re-read rows replace themselves

options.label: One day
options.description: For sources that write older timestamps, or a date-only change column

options.label: None
options.description: Reads only from the last sync onwards

defaults.reason: An hour catches rows committed late, and nothing doubles.

questions.text: Tables that already have rows in Fabric: skip them, or replace their rows?

options.label: Skip them
options.description: Data already there is never touched

options.label: Replace their rows
options.description: Each table is emptied, then loaded again

defaults.reason: Skipping never touches data already there, so a re-run is safe.

separateApprover.reason: It lets runs empty tables that already have rows in Fabric.

questions.text: Create and run the load pipelines, or only create them?

options.label: Create and run
options.description: The run waits for each load and compares row counts

options.label: Only create them
options.description: You run them from Fabric when you choose

defaults.reason: Running them lets the run compare row counts table by table.

questions.text: How many tables should the load pipeline copy at the same time?
questions.help: The load pipeline copies the tables in parallel batches. More is faster, and puts more load on the Synapse pool and the Fabric capacity at once. Fabric allows up to 50.

defaults.reason: Four at a time is fast, and gentle on a small pool.

questions.text: How should Fabric sign in to the Synapse pool to load data?
questions.help: Plan preselects it; any secret is still typed there, sent once with the run and never kept.

options.label: Workspace identity
options.description: No secret: a database admin grants the workspace's identity read access in the pool

options.label: SQL login, password in Key Vault
options.description: The secret stays in Azure Key Vault

options.label: Service principal, secret in Key Vault
options.description: The secret stays in Azure Key Vault

options.label: SQL login
options.description: The password is typed in Plan, once

options.label: Service principal
options.description: The secret is typed in Plan, once

defaults.reason: No secret passes through the accelerator.

questions.text: May object definitions be sent to Claude for drafts? Code only: never rows or credentials.
questions.help: Drafts are made only for the objects a person asks for (or the execution plan proposes, from this brief), and used only once a person accepts them. Each draft carries the migration context made from the approved brief (MIGRATION_CONTEXT.md). No keeps every model call off for this project, including help with these questions.

defaults.reason: Nothing leaves this machine unless a person says so.

separateApprover.reason: It allows object definitions to be sent to Claude, a service outside this machine.

questions.text: How much may this project spend on AI, in US dollars?
questions.help: Every model call's cost is counted against it. Once the spend reaches the budget, further calls are refused; the call that crosses it can go over by its own cost, which is shown before each draft.

defaults.reason: Enough for a few hundred drafts at typical prices.

questions.text: Multi-statement table-valued functions: draft them with AI, rewrite them by hand, or leave them out?
questions.help: Fabric Warehouse has no multi-statement table-valued functions. Each becomes an inline function or a view.

options.label: AI draft
options.description: The execution plan asks to draft each with Claude, for a person to review and accept

options.label: By hand
options.description: A task for a person, with the reason

options.label: Leave them out
options.description: Plan's Add all leaves them out

defaults.reason: {fact:code.multiStatementFunctions} functions, and AI drafts are allowed (D1).
{fact:code.multiStatementFunctions} functions, and no AI drafts (D1).

questions.text: Some columns are stored with less in Fabric (time keeps 6 fractional digits, datetimeoffset loses its offset, rowversion stops changing). Accept the mapped types, or have a person review those tables first?
questions.help: The mapping is fixed by what Fabric Warehouse can store (XML becomes text, spatial types become binary too), and Validate reports each changed type. Review adds a task to the execution plan, before any data loads.

options.label: Accept the mapped types
options.description: The closest type Fabric has, reported on each table

options.label: A person reviews those tables first
options.description: A task in the execution plan, before the data loads

defaults.reason: {fact:tables.lossyTypes} tables have such columns; each gets the closest type Fabric has.

questions.text: Procedures, views, functions and scripts that still use what Fabric rejects after the rules (such as FOR XML or RENAME OBJECT): draft them with AI, or rewrite them by hand?
questions.help: The rules fix what they can. The rest needs a rewrite: an AI draft a person reviews and accepts, or a person's own.

options.label: Draft them with AI
options.description: The execution plan asks to draft them; a person reviews and accepts each

options.label: Rewrite them by hand
options.description: A task for a person, with what Fabric rejects

defaults.reason: {fact:code.unconvertibleSql} objects, and AI drafts are allowed (D1).
{fact:code.unconvertibleSql} objects, and no AI drafts (D1).

questions.text: Which objects may be drafted with AI?
questions.help: Only what needs it keeps the definitions that convert cleanly on this machine. A person picks each object either way.

options.label: Only those the rules cannot convert
options.description: Multi-statement functions, code Fabric rejects, and objects with problems

options.label: Any object a person picks
options.description: Also those the rules convert, for a second opinion

defaults.reason: It sends the fewest definitions.

questions.text: .NET for Spark notebooks: rewrite them in which language?
questions.help: Fabric Spark runs Python, Scala, R and SQL, but not .NET (C#, F#). A rewrite, by AI or by hand, uses this language; drafts are told so.

options.label: PySpark (Python)
options.description: What most Fabric notebooks are written in

options.label: Scala
options.description: Closest to C# for a team that writes .NET

defaults.reason: {fact:code.dotnetNotebooks} notebooks use .NET; PySpark is what most Fabric notebooks are written in.

questions.text: Commit each run to the target workspace's Fabric Git branch?

defaults.reason: The target workspace is connected to Git: each run's items are committed, ready for a pull request.

questions.text: What should that commit take?

options.label: Only what the run made
options.description: Other changes waiting in the workspace are listed and left

options.label: Every change waiting in the workspace
options.description: Including changes someone else made in Fabric

defaults.reason: Other changes in the workspace are someone else's work, left for Fabric's Source control panel.

questions.text: What is the Fabric target workspace for?
questions.help: A production workspace raises every safeguard: each run waits for a person's sign-off, and the assistant never acts on its own there.

options.label: Development
options.description: Where the migration is built and tried

options.label: Test
options.description: Where the client's testers check it

options.label: Production
options.description: What the business runs on

defaults.reason: A migration is built in a development workspace first, then promoted.

questions.text: Which identity should create the items in Fabric, and so own them?
questions.help: Fabric makes the identity that creates an item its owner: schedules and pipelines then run with its access. Migrate creates items as the Fabric sign-in (Azure CLI or Fabric CLI); the execution plan checks it is this kind.

options.label: A person's account
options.description: The signed-in user; the simplest for a first migration

options.label: A service principal
options.description: Nothing depends on one person's account staying active

defaults.reason: Migrate signs in as a person today; a service principal is set up in Azure first.

questions.text: When must a person sign a run off before it writes to Fabric?

options.label: Never
options.description: The accelerator approves every run, and records it as its own

options.label: When it changes what Fabric already has
options.description: Updates in place, or rows replaced

options.label: Always
options.description: Every run waits for a person

defaults.reason: A production workspace: every run waits for a person.
A run that changes what Fabric already has waits for a person; any other is approved by the accelerator, and recorded as such.

separateApprover.reason: It lets every run write to Fabric without a person signing it off.

questions.text: Schedules: create them switched off, or switched on as they are in Synapse?
questions.help: A schedule that fires before its pipeline and the data it needs are ready does harm. Switched off, a person switches each on in Fabric when it is ready.

options.label: Switched off
options.description: A person switches each on in Fabric

options.label: As they are in Synapse
options.description: Switched on where the Synapse trigger was started

defaults.reason: {fact:triggers.schedule} schedule triggers; none runs before a person says so.

separateApprover.reason: It lets schedules run pipelines in Fabric as soon as they are created.

questions.text: Who sets up integration runtimes and event triggers, and switches the schedules on?
What may the assistant do on its own?
questions.help: The assistant follows the execution plan. It never approves anything, never accepts a draft and never enters a credential. On Act on Dev it may resume a run that was interrupted, and retry what failed for a passing reason (a timeout, throttling), a few times; everything else it asks a person for.

options.label: Observe
options.description: It reports and explains; it proposes nothing

options.label: Suggest
options.description: It proposes each action; a person confirms or rejects it

options.label: Act on Dev
options.description: On a development workspace only, it resumes and retries on its own

defaults.reason: It proposes; a person decides.

questions.text: What is the path to Test and Prod?

options.label: Dev only, for now
options.description: This migration targets the Dev workspace

options.label: Dev, then Test
options.description: Promoted from Git to Test

options.label: Dev, Test, then Prod
options.description: Promoted from Git through every environment, one at a time

defaults.reason: Deploying from Git to Test and Prod is not built yet: promotion is done from Fabric's deployment pipelines or Git, by a person.

questions.text: Which columns hold personal or sensitive data?
questions.help: Patterns of schema.table.column, matched ignoring case, with * for any text: sales.Customers.Email, *.*.ssn, hr.*.*. Drafts keep them out of logs, messages and copies (with G4's consent they are named to the AI); G1M can also mask them.

questions.text: Mask those columns in the Warehouse?
questions.help: A dynamic data mask shows people without UNMASK a masked value (xxxx, 0) instead of the data. Masks Synapse already has are kept either way.

options.label: Only the masks Synapse has
options.description: Nothing new is masked

options.label: Mask them
options.description: Each matching column without a mask gets the default mask

defaults.reason: Masking changes what people see: it is decided on purpose, not by default.

questions.text: Migrate roles and permissions?
questions.help: Roles, their members and GRANT / DENY permissions are recreated in the Warehouse. Masks travel with their tables either way.

defaults.reason: {fact:security.roles} roles and the permissions of {fact:security.principals} roles and users can be recreated in the Warehouse.

questions.text: Which Microsoft Entra user or group replaces each SQL user?
questions.help: Fabric has no SQL authentication. A mapped SQL user's permissions and role memberships go to the Microsoft Entra principal instead. One left blank stays listed for a person, with the statements to run.

defaults.reason: None mapped: {fact:security.sqlUsers} SQL users stay listed for a person.

questions.text: Where must the data stay? A region, such as West Europe
questions.help: The Fabric capacity's region decides where OneLake keeps the data. The execution plan checks the target workspace's capacity against this before anything is written.

questions.text: What may go to Claude with each draft, besides the object's own definition?
questions.help: The migration context makes drafts follow this brief: its decisions and standards, the sensitive columns, the context answers (I1 to I5), and the columns of the objects the draft reads. Minimal sends only the decisions that shape the code.

options.label: The migration context
options.description: MIGRATION_CONTEXT.md in full, and the columns of what the object reads

options.label: Only the decisions
options.description: No context answers, no names of sensitive columns or Entra principals, no columns of other objects

defaults.reason: Drafts follow the brief best with all of it; each draft records which context file it was made with.

questions.text: How should linked services' connections sign in by default?
questions.help: Plan preselects it for each linked service. Neither option passes a secret through the accelerator.

options.label: Workspace identity
options.description: The Fabric workspace's own identity, granted access to each service

options.label: A secret in Azure Key Vault
options.description: Through a Fabric Azure Key Vault reference

defaults.reason: {fact:linkedServices.keyVault} linked services already read their secrets from Azure Key Vault.
No secret passes through the accelerator.

questions.text: How deep should Validate check by default?

options.label: Compare only
options.description: Definitions, columns and row counts

options.label: Also query and compile
options.description: Tables and views are queried, procedures compiled; nothing changes

options.label: Also run them
options.description: Pipelines, notebooks and Spark jobs really run in Fabric

defaults.reason: Querying and compiling proves objects work without changing anything.

questions.text: Run Synapse and Fabric side by side before cutover?
questions.help: Both run on their schedules for a few cycles, and their results are compared before Synapse is switched off. The execution plan adds a task for each cycle.

defaults.reason: A production cutover is proved by running both side by side.
A development workspace is not cut over: decide this for the production migration.

questions.text: For how many cycles?

defaults.reason: Three cycles catch most differences that come and go.

questions.text: What is the cutover window, and what does a rollback mean?
Do the pipelines and notebooks write to systems outside Fabric that are in production (databases, files, APIs)?
questions.help: Validate's deepest check really runs pipelines, notebooks and Spark jobs in Fabric. Against production systems that writes real data; against test copies of them it is safe.

options.label: No, or only to test copies
options.description: Running them in Validate is safe

options.label: Yes, to production systems
options.description: Validate does not run them unless a person says why

options.label: Not sure
options.description: Treated as yes until someone checks

defaults.reason: Nobody has checked yet: until someone does, Validate does not run them.

questions.text: What is the timeline?
questions.help: Sent to the AI with each draft as context (G4), and kept in the brief for the team.

questions.text: What hurts today (slow loads, costs, failures)?
questions.help: Drafts favour what fixes it, without changing what the code does.

questions.text: What reads the data downstream (Power BI reports, applications)?
questions.help: Drafts keep the names and shapes these depend on.

questions.text: What does the team know best (T-SQL, PySpark, Scala)?
questions.help: Code a draft has to add is written the way the team can look after it.

questions.text: Who approves the migration?
questions.help: Kept in the brief for the team; never sent to the AI.

conflicts.message: Data loads into the Warehouse's tables, which Structure creates. Without it the loads fail, unless the tables are already in Fabric.

resolutions.label: Keep my answer: the tables are already in Fabric

conflicts.message: Replacing rows empties tables that already have data, and no person would sign such a run off first.

resolutions.label: Sign off runs that change what Fabric has
resolutions.question: E4

conflicts.message: AI drafts need consent to send definitions to Claude (D1).
The pool ({fact:pool.collation}) compares names and text case-insensitively. Code that relies on that, such as a join of 'ABC' with 'abc', behaves differently in a case-sensitive Warehouse.

resolutions.label: Keep case-sensitive: the code was checked

conflicts.message: This brief rests on a discovery that could not read: {fact:discovery.failedCategories}. Run discovery again, or go on knowing it.
Updating objects in place overwrites changes someone made in Fabric, and no person would sign such a run off first.

resolutions.label: Sign off runs that change what Fabric has
resolutions.question: E4

conflicts.message: AI drafts need consent to send definitions to Claude (D1).
A production workspace: every run waits for a person's sign-off there, whatever E4 says.

resolutions.label: Keep the answers: production signs off every run anyway

conflicts.message: Validate would really run pipelines and notebooks that may write to production systems (H4).

resolutions.label: Keep running them: they write to test copies, or that is intended

conflicts.message: The assistant acts on its own only on a development workspace; on this one it will ask a person for everything.

resolutions.label: Keep the answers: it acts alone once a development workspace is the target

history.note: Re-lettered to follow the MNP consultation's sections (A scope, B target, C data, D code, E operations, G security, H validation, I context).
